2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Moderate risk: In an unbalanced panel of 44 countries over 14 years (616 potential country-years), baseline models retain 541 observations (~12% missing) and models with foreign aid and FDI retain 513 observations (~17% missing). Forward orthogonal deviations are used to mitigate observation loss from panel gaps, but patterns and causes of missing country-years are not analyzed.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Serious risk: Benchmark two-step system-GMM regressions treat institutional quality as strictly exogenous and omit time fixed effects; several specifications (Tables 2, 3, and 6) yield explosive lagged dependent variable coefficients exceeding 1.0, and specifications treating institutions as endogenous via internal lags suffer from instrument proliferation (country-to-instrument ratio r < 1). As the authors explicitly state on p. 17, the aggregate design does not establish causality.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Weak / low specificity: Legal and institutional variables (including Rule of Law and Regulatory Quality) are operationalized solely via aggregate Worldwide Governance Indicators (WGI) subjective perception scores (-2.5 to 2.5 and percentile ranks) rather than coding formal sanitation statutes, regulatory agencies, or de jure legal rules; as acknowledged on p. 13 (citing Rodrik 2004), WGI captures investor and survey perceptions rather than specific formal institutional designs.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Serious risk: Institutional exposures rely on subjective perception-based WGI composites vulnerable to halo effects and reverse causality from broader economic and public-service performance, while sanitation outcomes rely on highly persistent interpolated national/rural/urban aggregate series (first-lag correlation of 0.99).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate / macro-standardized only: Access to improved sanitation (AIS) is consistently defined across national, rural, and urban series as the percentage of the population with access to and using improved sanitation facilities, but relies on smoothed aggregate country-year statistics (lag-1 correlation = 0.99) without household-level verification of facility functionality or explicit primary database citations in the main text (deferred to online Appendix).
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: No information (no pre-analysis plan or protocol exists), though selective reporting concern is partially mitigated by extensive sensitivity reporting across all six WGI dimensions, percentile ranks, three composite indices, domestic vs. foreign control sets, time fixed effects, endogenous GMM specifications, and rural/urban splits (Tables 2-9).
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Moderate risk: The sample includes 44 Sub-Saharan African countries over 2002-2015 selected on data availability (excluding several SSA states and missing country-years, with the country list deferred to online Appendix B), creating potential under-representation of fragile or conflict-affected jurisdictions lacking governance, aid, or sanitation statistics.

domain_ratings.justification: Although the authors use two-step system GMM (Blundell and Bond 1998) with country fixed effects and domestic/foreign macroeconomic controls, benchmark regressions (Tables 2-5, 8) treat institutional quality as strictly exogenous and omit time fixed effects during the MDG era. Adding foreign controls or time fixed effects yields unstable lagged dependent variable estimates exceeding unity (>1.0) in multiple columns (Tables 3 and 6), violating dynamic stability. When institutional quality is treated as endogenous using internal lagged instruments (Table 7), the instrument count exceeds the number of countries (r < 1), weakening the Hansen J test for instrument validity. No external quasi-experimental shock is exploited, and the authors explicitly conclude (p. 17) that the study does not establish causality between institutions and sanitation.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section III (PDF pp. 7-8); Section IV, Tables 2-7 (PDF pp. 8-14); Section VI (PDF p. 17)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domain_ratings.justification: The study analyzes an unbalanced panel of 44 Sub-Saharan African countries from 2002 to 2015 (541 observations in domestic specifications; 513 with foreign controls), with the country list placed in online Supporting Information (Table B.2). Inclusion of countries and country-years appears driven by secondary data availability across WGI, sanitation, and aid datasets rather than outcome-dependent selection directly, but omission of SSA states/years lacking data (typically conflict-affected or fragile states with weak institutions and low sanitation coverage) introduces moderate selection risk.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section II, Table 1 & fn. 5 (PDF pp. 4-5); Figure 2 (PDF p. 3); Tables 2-3 (PDF pp. 10-11)

domain_ratings.justification: Rather than measuring discrete legal or institutional reforms, institutional quality is operationalized as continuous perception scores from the six Worldwide Governance Indicators (WGI). As the authors acknowledge in Section IV.D (p. 13, citing Rodrik 2004), WGI indicators reflect surveys of domestic and foreign investors/experts capturing subjective perceptions rather than formal aspects of institutional design, and perceptions are shaped by broader economic and public-service conditions—creating reverse-causality/endogeneity contamination in classifying institutional quality.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section II.A & II.C (PDF pp. 5-7); Section IV.D (PDF p. 13)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domain_ratings.justification: In this observational macro-panel context, concurrent national and donor co-interventions during the 2002-2015 MDG push for sanitation could co-vary with governance indicators. The authors partially account for co-interventions by controlling for general government consumption expenditure (% GDP) in all models and targeted foreign aid to water and sanitation (% GDP) in extended models (Table 3, Table 7, Table 8, Table 9), though benchmark models omit foreign aid and subnational/NGO sanitation programs are unmeasured.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section I (PDF pp. 1-2); Section II.B (PDF pp. 6-7); Section IV, Tables 2-3 (PDF pp. 9-11)

domain_ratings.justification: Across 44 countries and 14 years (616 potential country-years), 541 observations are available in domestic regressions (~12.2% missing) and 513 when adding water/sanitation aid and FDI (~16.7% missing), and sector-specific sanitation aid had to be replaced with combined water-and-sanitation aid due to missing data across years (p. 7). The authors appropriately apply forward orthogonal deviations (Arellano and Bover 1995) to preserve sample size in unbalanced panels with gaps, but do not test whether missingness is systematically related to governance collapse or low sanitation access.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section II.B (PDF p. 7); Section III & fn. 7 (PDF p. 8); Tables 2-6 (PDF pp. 10-14)

domain_ratings.justification: Access to improved sanitation (AIS)—overall, rural, and urban—is measured via standardized international development definitions (% of population with access and using improved sanitation facilities). Because these series are compiled externally prior to the study, differential assessor bias is unlikely; however, exact primary source citations for AIS are omitted from the main text (deferred to online Appendix), and national annual sanitation figures rely heavily on interpolated household surveys, reflected in the 0.99 first-lag correlation reported on p. 8, which introduces smoothing measurement error in annual dynamic panel estimation.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section II, Table 1 (PDF pp. 4-5); Section III (PDF p. 8); Section V (PDF pp. 14-16)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias in selection of the reported result
domain_ratings.justification: No pre-analysis plan or pre-registered protocol exists for this observational econometric study, so pre-specification of model lag limits, control sets, and composite functional forms cannot be verified (rated No information per ROBINS-I guidance when no protocol exists). Within the published paper, the authors report results transparently across all six WGI dimensions (including non-significant indicators), percentile ranks, three composite indices, time fixed effects, endogenous institution specifications, and rural/urban decompositions.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section III (PDF p. 8); Section IV, Tables 2-7 & fn. 13 (PDF pp. 9-14); Section V, Tables 8-9 (PDF pp. 14-16)

evidence_quotes.quote: However, in the robustness exercise, quality of institutions is assumed to be endogenous.

Moreover, as Rodrik (2004) points out, the most commonly used institutional quality measures are based on surveys of domestic and foreign investors, thus capturing perceptions rather than any of the formal aspects of the institutional setting.

evidence_quotes.quote: Despite limiting the number of lags used in the GMM-style instruments, treating institutions as endogenous naturally increases the number of instruments.
However, the study depends on aggregated data and does not establish causality between institutions and sanitation.

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Study S1036 (Francois, Kakeu, and Kouame 2021) is an observational longitudinal country-year dynamic panel econometric analysis of 44 Sub-Saharan African countries over 2002-2015 using two-step system GMM (Blundell and Bond 1998) to estimate the effect of institutional governance quality (six Worldwide Governance Indicators) on national, rural, and urban access to improved sanitation. Appraised under ROBINS-I, the study is judged at Serious overall risk of bias, driven primarily by Domain 1 (confounding) and Domain 3 (classification/measurement of institutional exposures). Specifically, baseline models treat institutional quality as strictly exogenous and omit time fixed effects; several extended specifications exhibit explosive lagged dependent variable coefficients (>1.0); and specifications instrumenting endogenous institutions with internal lags exceed the safe instrument-to-country ratio (r < 1), weakening overidentification tests without any external quasi-experimental source of variation. Furthermore, institutional exposures are measured exclusively through subjective WGI perception composites rather than formal sanitation laws or de jure regulatory institutions, which—as the authors themselves acknowledge—are susceptible to simultaneity with broader economic conditions and cannot establish causality or isolate specific legal mechanisms. Selection into the unbalanced 44-country panel, MDG-era co-interventions, missing country-year observations (~12%-17%), and smoothed aggregate sanitation series pose Moderate concerns, while no pre-analysis plan is reported (No information for D7).
raw_response.study_design_identified: Observational longitudinal country-year dynamic panel econometric study (44 Sub-Saharan African countries, 2002-2015) using two-step system Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) with internal lagged instruments
raw_response.where_found_summary: Full text of the 18-page published article read: Abstract & Section I Introduction (PDF pp. 1-4); Section II Data and Variables of Interest & Table 1 (PDF pp. 4-7); Section III Estimation Procedure (PDF pp. 7-8); Section IV Results & Robustness Regressions, Tables 2-7 (PDF pp. 8-14); Section V Rural versus Urban Analysis, Tables 8-9 (PDF pp. 14-16); Section VI Concluding Remarks (PDF pp. 16-17). Note: Online Supporting Information (Appendix S1, containing country list Table B.2 and full appendix regression tables) is referenced on PDF p. 18 as external online material and is not appended to the article PDF.
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The study estimates the direct impact of institutional governance quality on access to improved sanitation across a comparative longitudinal panel of 44 countries (2002-2015) using dynamic panel system-GMM internal instrumental-variable estimation and policy counterfactuals (e.g., DR Congo vs. Mauritius). Under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, ROBINS-I is the designated instrument for non-randomized comparative longitudinal/panel and IV-type econometric evaluations of policy/institutional exposures.
